node.name: Daily Worship at Marquand Chapel
node.descriptionText:
Join us at 11:30am in Marquand Chapel for our daily worship.

Worship in Marquand often draws on a wide variety of inherited Christian traditions, with the worship of many denominations being represented. Beyond that, though, we also pay attention to the rising number of people in Western society who have a lively interest in spirituality but feel no connection to traditional forms of church and worship. So Marquand is also actively engaged in original, creative, and experimental forms of worship, both for committed Christians and for those exploring the faith.

node.name: BIOMES: "Sustainable AI – is it possible?" presented by Elaine Grunewald, Lecturer, Yale School of the Environment
node.descriptionText:
About the Seminar:
The AI value chain is extensive, complex and varied, ranging from minerals and materials, to hardware to infrastructure to models and user applications. There are distinct sustainability issues across this chain. Often the public associates AI sustainability issues to be data center centric, when in fact the picture is far more complex, encompassing energy and water issues, but also the profound effects on people, the economy and society more broadly.  At the same time, the magnitude of the sustainability challenges we face, and the fact that we have exceeded several planetary boundaries - ranging from climate change to oceans to biodiversity – will likely require AI to solve.  This talk will breakdown the issues, and outline the two sides of the sustainability AI coin – risk and opportunity – from a business lens, building on Elaine’s more than 2 decades of experience in the corporate sustainability space.

About the Speaker:
Elaine is a global operating executive with more than 25 years of experience leading technology-driven organizations through growth, transformation, and complexity across multinational, start up, and board environments. Her focus is on tech and digitalization, venture building and investing, public affairs and partnerships, and corporate development. Her advocacy for the private sector’s role in solving sustainability challenges has been a red thread throughout her career. 

She has held senior executive roles at scale, including Senior Vice President and Executive Team member at Ericsson, where she led global sustainability, public affairs, and stakeholder strategy and built an organization of 150+ professionals operating across regulated and geopolitically complex markets. In that role, she worked closely with the Board, CEO, investors, governments, and customers, positioning sustainability, trust, and responsible technology as drivers of long-term competitiveness and growth.

More recently, she served as President of the Tonomus Venture Studio, the venture-building arm of NEOM, Saudi Arabia’s future-focused development. She led a global, multidisciplinary team responsible for building and launching a portfolio of AI- and data-driven ventures. Using a hands-on operating model, her team incubated and scaled early-stage companies across sectors including fintech and digital identity, workforce authentication, biotech, satellite-enabled services, climate tech, and responsible AI.

Elaine co-founded two companies - the AI Sustainability Center, developing practical tools to help companies address the scaling of Responsible AI, and Emphco AB, a platform she uses to advise numerous companies, funds and CEOs and to make clean tech investments.  

Alongside operating roles, she brings board and capital-markets experience, having served on public company boards and as an independent director of a Nasdaq-listed SPAC. Non-profit boards include the Whitaker Peace & Development Initiative & the International Women’s Forum Sweden.    

She is the co-author of the book Sustainability Leadership, a Swedish Approach to Transforming Your Company, Your Industry and the World (2020, Palgrave Macmillan). She was also a contributor to the anthology Ethics at Work: Dilemmas of the Near Future and How Your Organization Can Solve Them (2022).  Elaine is a frequent speaker including the World Economic Forum, United Nations, LEAP, SXSW, tech industry events and has been engaged in the Broadband Commission for Sustainable Development, and the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network. She has held guest lectures at multiple universities including Columbia University Business School and Sweden’s Royal Institute of Technology (KTH) Business School.  She has received several awards for her work with sustainability and women's leadership.

node.name: Spiritually Equipping Children and Youth During Difficult Times with the Rev. Deshna Charron
node.descriptionText:
Zoom | November 11 | 12 – 1:30 pm Eastern

Around the world, communities are facing major social and systemic change. Signs of societal and environmental collapse are evident. Our attempts to live “independently,” create the experience of separation that leads to suffering, division and destruction, all of which runs counter to the sacred teachings present in all the World Religions, Earth-centered expressions and the teachings of Jesus. Nourishing children spiritually and equipping them with the skills they need to not just survive but thrive within this chaotic and stressful environment can ground, prepare, and inspire the next generation. We do this by providing spiritual practices, self-awareness exercises, and organizing tools so that youth and their communities may rise up resiliently, modeling a healthy, and whole way forward for all.

node.name: Interwoven: Sounds and Visions from the World’s Refugee Camps
node.descriptionText:
This retrospective exhibition of community art and traditional music will be on view at the Yale Institute of Sacred Music’s Miller Hall at 406 Prospect Street, New Haven from October 15 -December 3 on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays from 12 - 4 p.m., except for Thanksgiving week when the ISM is closed.

Presented by Artolution, an international community-based public arts, education, and mental health organization that uses creative expression to build connection, resilience, and community, the exhibition is organized by Dr. Max Frieder, Artolution Co-Founder and Chief Creative Officer (read more about Dr. Frieder below).

Building on the acclaimed exhibition Interwoven: Exchange Artworks Made Between Refugee Camps Around the World, originally launched at the United Nations, this expanded presentation hosted at the ISM brings together large-scale collaborative artworks, video documentation of traditional folkloric musicians, and cultural artifacts created by displaced communities across five continents.

The exhibition creates a dialogue between visual art and music in contexts of displacement and crisis. Alongside the artworks, visitors encounter videos of musicians from the same communities, offering an opportunity to experience not only the remarkable stories behind the works, but also the sounds, movements, languages, rhythms, and creative traditions of the people who made them.

Together, these works offer a powerful portrait of communities using art, music, and cultural expression to preserve identity, share their stories, and create connections across borders.

Social Security faces long-term fiscal challenges, raising fundamental questions about what the program should aim to provide and how it should be financed. node.name: LPE Workshop Series: AI, Tech, and Cloud Computing with Asad Ramzanali
node.descriptionText:
Please join us for the fifth session of the LPE Fall Workshop Series, Economic Governance in a Post-Neoliberal Age: Networks, Platforms, and Utilities (NPU) Law and Other Approaches. The session will be Wednesday, November 11th, from 4:40-6:00pm. Asad Ramzanali, Director of Artificial Intelligence and Technology Policy at the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator, will present a forthcoming paper on NPU approaches to AI and tech regulation. 

More on the Workshop Series:
Rapid technological and economic changes, political uncertainty, and climate change have supercharged longstanding challenges associated with concentrated private power across politics and the economy, raising new and urgent questions for the future of economic governance and our democracy. At the heart of many of these challenges lie industries known as networks, platforms, and utilities (NPUs)—economic sectors crucial for the functioning of the broader economy, such as finance, energy, communications, and transportation. The NPU speaker series will host distinguished scholars as they present their research and new perspectives on tools to regulate NPU industries from finance to AI to energy.

node.name: Edward P. Bass Distinguished Lecture: "Homesick for a World Unknown" with Miriam Horn
node.descriptionText:
Beginning in the 1950s with Congo's mountain gorillas, field biologist George Schaller revolutionized wildlife science by going to live with Earth’s most feared and revered creatures, from the great cats (tigers, lions, snow leopards, jaguars) to pandas, Tibetan brown bears, Gobi wild camels and many more. Before Jane Goodall or Dian Fossey, he was the first to reveal these primates and predators’ rich emotional and social lives, and to commit his science to ensuring their survival: studying whole ecosystems to understand the animals’ needs, helping to create national parks that together protect an area the size of France, and mentoring generations of biologists on four continents.

Instrumental to those breakthroughs were the rigorous and beautiful field notes and journals Schaller kept every day for more than seven decades, preserving an hour-by-hour account of his acute perceptions, perilous adventures, political strategizing and closely guarded interior life. Entrusted to the Yale Peabody Museum, along with a century of correspondence and family albums, those archives proved indispensable to biographer Miriam Horn, whose Homesick for a World Unknown, The Life of George B. Schaller, was published in April by Penguin Press. In a talk illustrated with Schaller’s groundbreaking photographs and drawings – including the first-ever films shot of wild gorillas, also preserved at Yale—Horn will trace the dramatic story she spent eight years in the archives working to bring to light. 

Books will be for sale from 4 to 5 pm and Horn will be on hand for a signing from 4:15 pm to 4:45 pm. 
“Before Jane Goodall or Dian Fossey, he was the first to reveal these primates and predators’ rich emotional and social lives,” said Miriam Horn, author of Homesick for a World Unknown: The Life of George B. Schaller, the first biography of Schaller, the preeminent field biologist of the past century.

Horn will offer a talk illustrated with Schaller’s groundbreaking photographs and drawings - including the first-ever films shot of wild gorillas, also preserved at Yale - tracting the dramatic story she spent eight years in the archives working to bring to light.

Horn’s Edward P. Bass Distinguished Lecture will take place Wednesday, November 11 at 5 pm in O.C. Marsh Hall. The event is free and open to the public. The lecture is co-sponsored by the Yale Peabody Museum and the Yale Institute for Biospheric Studies. Books will be on sale at the event.

“Schaller committed his science to ensuring their survival: studying whole ecosystems to understand the animals’ needs, helping to create national parks that together protect an area the size of France, and mentoring generations of biologists on four continents,” Horn said.

Instrumental to those breakthroughs were the rigorous and beautiful field notes and journals Schaller kept every day for more than seven decades, preserving an hour-by-hour account of his acute perceptions, perilous adventures, political strategizing and closely guarded interior life.

Schaller’s field notes and journals were entrusted to the Yale Peabody Museum, along with a century of correspondence and family albums. Those archives proved indispensable to Horn, whose biography of Schaller, was published in April by Penguin Press.

Horn is an author, environmental advocate, journalist and filmmaker. Her previous books include Rebels in White Gloves: Coming of Age with Hillary’s Class; the New York Times bestselling Earth: The Sequel: The Race to Reinvent Energy and Stop Global Warming; and Rancher, Farmer, Fisherman: Conservation Heroes of the American Heartland. Two were made into documentary films for the Discovery Channel, with Horn acting as producer, and a Sundance premiere.

Horn spent fifteen years at the Environmental Defense Fund and six years at the U.S. Forest Service in Colorado, working on habitat conservation, landowner and community partnerships, and public education. Before joining EDF, she was a senior writer at U.S. News and World Report and freelanced for many years for the New York Times and other publications.

node.name: Dark Waters Screening & Talk with Dr. Robert Bilott: The Lawyer Behind the Story
node.descriptionText:
The Yale Environmental Law Association (YELA) is excited to welcome Dr. Robert Bilott for a screening of Dark Waters (2019), followed by a moderated Q&A with Dr. Bilott himself!

Based on the true story of Bilott’s decades-long legal battle against chemical giant DuPont, Dark Waters follows an environmental attorney who takes on the case of a West Virginia farmer whose cattle are mysteriously dying. His investigation uncovers widespread water contamination linked to DuPont’s disposal of PFOA (C8), a toxic “forever chemical” used in the production of Teflon. What begins as a local environmental complaint grows into a landmark legal battle over corporate accountability, public health, and environmental justice.

Join us for the screening and a rare opportunity to hear directly from the attorney behind the story about the litigation, the challenges he faced, and the real events that inspired the film!

node.name: Pure and Impure Thoughts: A Homodoxy Seminar
node.descriptionText:
Think queerly. Read deeply. Be in community.

Pure and Impure Thoughts is a monthly reading and discussion seminar from Homodoxy exploring theological, sexual, political, and social meanings of purity and impurity across religious traditions and genres—particularly as they relate to gay, queer, and trans lives and loves.

Conversation is informal, exploratory, and engaged, and readings vary in length and difficulty.

Fall 2026 readings:
September 9 — Indecent Theology: Theological Perversions in Sex, Gender, and Politics by Marcella Althaus-Reid
October 14 — The Trouble with Normal: Sex, Politics, and the Ethics of Queer Life by Michael Warner
November 11 — Reading to be announced
December 9 — Reading to be announced

The seminar meets from 6:00–8:00 PM at the New Haven Pride Center, 50 Orange St., New Haven. Participation is free. Homodoxy notes that the readings and discussion are most appropriate for ages 18+.

Organized by Homodoxy and led by Yale alum Samuel Ernest, Ph.D. RSVP through Homodoxy to receive information about the readings.

The Yale LGBTQ Center is sharing this event on behalf of Homodoxy.

  • No registration required for Yale students, faculty, and staff to attend but they will need to be 21+ to get in and should bring their government IDs.

Enjoy the vibes with light bites and beverages from The Well and you can also order burgers on Wednesdays!
